variants.title: Narrow the claim to evidence
variants.context: A knowledge benchmark turns a broad claim into bounded evidence in four stages: define the claim, build the blueprint, freeze the protocol, then qualify the result. Every stage narrows what the final score may honestly claim.
variants.prompt: A team wants to advertise that its assistant answers current product policy questions. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Qualify the result: report slice evidence, uncertainty, contamination checks, and the use the score supports.
Define the claim: name the users, topics, authoritative sources, knowledge cutoff, languages, tools, and consequences.
Build the blueprint: allocate protected items across domains, operations, difficulty, formats, and critical slices.
Freeze the protocol: pin prompts, retrieval access, tools, sampling, answer format, graders, and versions.

variants.hint: The item budget is allocated before anyone looks at a model result.
variants.explanation: Each stage narrows the claim, so the score can support only what its items, protocol, and slices represent.

variants.title: Narrow the claim to evidence
variants.context: A knowledge benchmark turns a broad claim into bounded evidence in four stages: define the claim, build the blueprint, freeze the protocol, then qualify the result. Every stage narrows what the final score may honestly claim.
variants.prompt: The same assistant is extended to Spanish. Put the stages in order for the new language claim.

items.text: Qualify the result: report the Spanish slices with their intervals and limit the claim to those counts.
Freeze the protocol: pin the Spanish prompts, retrieval access, answer format, graders, and model version.
Define the claim: state that Spanish support questions are in scope and name the Spanish sources and cutoff date.
Build the blueprint: reserve minimum item counts for the Spanish cells, including the critical exception-handling slice.

variants.hint: A new language is a new population, not a new prompt.
variants.explanation: A claim covering a language needs its own items, protocol, and slice evidence before the score can mention it.

variants.title: Narrow the claim to evidence
variants.context: A knowledge benchmark turns a broad claim into bounded evidence in four stages: define the claim, build the blueprint, freeze the protocol, then qualify the result. Every stage narrows what the final score may honestly claim.
variants.prompt: The retrieval index is rebuilt on a fresher source snapshot. Put the stages in order for the re-measurement.

items.text: Freeze the protocol: repin retrieval access, tools, graders, and versions against the new index snapshot.
Qualify the result: rerun the gate and report the date-compliance slice before extending the claim.
Build the blueprint: check that the protected items still cover the domains and operations the new sources touch.
Define the claim: restate the time boundary and source set the refreshed index is meant to answer for.

variants.hint: Changing what the system can retrieve changes what the old score measured.
variants.explanation: An index change alters the measured system, so the claim, blueprint coverage, protocol, and gate are all revisited.

variants.title: Operate the versioned suite
variants.context: The suite is operated as a versioned measurement product in four steps: author and review items, calibrate scoring, run and preserve the protocol, then analyze and decide. Fixtures are re-run whenever any input to the measurement changes.
variants.prompt: A new knowledge suite is being stood up for the first time. Put the operating steps in order.

items.text: Calibrate scoring: build deterministic fixtures or a rubric set, measure reviewer agreement, and pin grader versions.
Author and review: write from the blueprint, verify source authority and dates, and protect the final split.
Run and preserve: execute the frozen model, prompt, retrieval, tools, and limits, retaining raw outputs, errors, and cost.
Analyze and decide: review aggregate and slice results, uncertainty, prompt sensitivity, and contamination before the gate.

variants.hint: Scoring is validated before a run is interpreted, not after.
variants.explanation: Authoring, calibration, execution, and analysis are separate steps so a scoring defect cannot be mistaken for model behavior.

variants.title: Operate the versioned suite
variants.context: The suite is operated as a versioned measurement product in four steps: author and review items, calibrate scoring, run and preserve the protocol, then analyze and decide. Fixtures are re-run whenever any input to the measurement changes.
variants.prompt: An automated grader is replaced with a new rubric. Put the steps in order for the re-run.

items.text: Analyze and decide: compare the regraded slices with the previous run before letting the gate use either number.
Calibrate scoring: score an overlapping sample with blinded human reviewers and record agreement by slice.
Author and review: confirm the protected items and their keys are unchanged by the rubric edit.
Run and preserve: rescore the retained raw outputs under the pinned new grader version.

variants.hint: Ask what changed: the model, or the instrument measuring it.
variants.explanation: A grader change is a new measurement version, so agreement is recalibrated and the old and new scores are compared explicitly.

variants.title: Operate the versioned suite
variants.context: The suite is operated as a versioned measurement product in four steps: author and review items, calibrate scoring, run and preserve the protocol, then analyze and decide. Fixtures are re-run whenever any input to the measurement changes.
variants.prompt: A model upgrade arrives the week before a release review. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Run and preserve: execute the upgraded model under the frozen protocol and keep every failure record.
Analyze and decide: apply the release gate to slices, uncertainty, and prompt sensitivity, not to the headline alone.
Author and review: verify the protected split is still unexposed and rotate any item family under suspicion.
Calibrate scoring: re-run the golden item, parser, and scorer fixtures so scoring defects surface first.

variants.hint: Fixtures run before the candidate does.
variants.explanation: Re-running fixtures first separates a scoring regression from a model regression when the headline moves.

variants.title: Size a blueprint cell
variants.context: A blueprint allocates a fixed item budget across domains and cognitive operations. One cell holds the budget times the domain share times the operation share. Standard cells need at least 20 items and critical cells at least 40.
variants.prompt: A support copilot blueprint has an 800 item budget. Security holds a 20 percent domain share and the apply operation holds a 35 percent share. How many items does the security apply cell receive?
variants.hint: Both shares apply to the same budget, one after the other.
variants.explanation: A cell holds the budget times the domain share times the operation share, so 800 times 0.20 times 0.35 gives 56 items, above the 40 item critical minimum.

mistakes.feedback: That applies the domain share only and ignores the operation mix.
That applies the operation share only and ignores which domain the cell belongs to.

variants.title: Size a blueprint cell
variants.context: A blueprint allocates a fixed item budget across domains and cognitive operations. One cell holds the budget times the domain share times the operation share. Standard cells need at least 20 items and critical cells at least 40.
variants.prompt: A 600 item budget gives escalation a 10 percent domain share, and the apply operation holds 35 percent. Escalation apply is a critical cell. How many items does it receive?
variants.hint: Compute the cell first, then compare it with the minimum it must clear.
variants.explanation: 600 times 0.10 times 0.35 is 21 items, which is below the 40 item critical minimum, so the cell must be refilled or the claim narrowed.

mistakes.feedback: That stops at the domain share and never applies the operation mix.
That applies the operation share to the whole budget instead of to the escalation slice.

variants.title: Size a blueprint cell
variants.context: A blueprint allocates a fixed item budget across domains and cognitive operations. One cell holds the budget times the domain share times the operation share. Standard cells need at least 20 items and critical cells at least 40.
variants.prompt: A policy assistant blueprint has a 1200 item budget. Eligibility holds a 25 percent domain share and the explain operation holds 15 percent. How many items land in eligibility explain?
variants.hint: Multiply the budget by both shares before judging whether the cell is thin.
variants.explanation: 1200 times 0.25 times 0.15 is 45 items, which clears the 20 item standard minimum but leaves little room for a slice interval.

mistakes.feedback: That is the whole eligibility domain, not the explain cell inside it.
That is every explain item across all domains, not the eligibility share of them.

variants.title: Bound what the score claims
variants.context: A score supports only the claim its items, protocol, scoring rules, and slices represent. Closed-book and open-book results answer different questions, unexpected jumps are audit triggers, and failures stay in the denominator.
variants.prompt: A model scores 91 percent closed book on product facts, but the grounded slice with supplied sources sits at 58 percent and its citations often point at superseded pages. What does this evidence support?
options: A retrieval defect only, so the headline can be published once the index refresh lands next quarter.
Broad familiarity with product facts, with no support for a claim about using current supplied sources.
Reliable current-policy answering, because the closed-book score shows the knowledge is already in the model.
optionFeedback: Naming a cause does not restore evidence; the current claim still fails on the slice that was actually measured.
Correct: the closed-book result bounds the parameter knowledge claim and the weak grounded slice blocks the evidence-use claim.
Closed-book recall says nothing about whether the system finds and respects the supplied, dated evidence.
variants.hint: Closed book and open book answer different questions.
variants.explanation: Closed book probes what parameters and the prompt produce, while open book measures the whole system finding and using supplied evidence, so a weak grounded slice bounds the claim.

variants.title: Bound what the score claims
variants.context: A score supports only the claim its items, protocol, scoring rules, and slices represent. Closed-book and open-book results answer different questions, unexpected jumps are audit triggers, and failures stay in the denominator.
variants.prompt: After a training-data refresh, one public item family jumps 24 points while freshly rewritten variants of the same concepts stay flat. What is the defensible reading?
options: Treat the gap as an exposure signal and audit item provenance and near-duplicate overlap before reporting a gain.
Report the improvement, since the rewritten variants are simply a harder benchmark with a different baseline.
Average the familiar items and the rewritten variants so the headline reflects both versions of the concept.
optionFeedback: Correct: an unexpectedly large gain on protected items is an audit trigger, not automatic proof of new capability.
The variants preserve the concept and change only surface form, so the gap points at familiarity rather than difficulty.
Averaging hides the exact contrast that revealed the problem and publishes a number nobody can interpret.
variants.hint: Ask what changed: the capability, or the familiarity of the surface form.
variants.explanation: Controlled variants preserve the concept while changing surface form, so a jump on the original items alone signals contamination and starts an overlap audit.

variants.title: Bound what the score claims
variants.context: A score supports only the claim its items, protocol, scoring rules, and slices represent. Closed-book and open-book results answer different questions, unexpected jumps are audit triggers, and failures stay in the denominator.
variants.prompt: Twelve percent of attempts returned parse errors and were dropped before scoring, which lifted reported accuracy from 79 to 88 percent. What should the report do?
options: Keep the parse errors in the attempted-item denominator and publish 79 percent with the failure breakdown.
Publish 88 percent as the model quality figure and track parse errors as a separate engineering defect.
Rerun only the failed items with a repaired parser and merge those results into the original run.
optionFeedback: Correct: refusals, parse errors, and tool failures stay in the attempted-item denominator so the score matches the served behavior.
Dropping failures measures a system that never fails to answer, which is not the system users receive.
Patching only the failed subset mixes two protocols and produces a score that cannot be reproduced.
variants.hint: Which denominator matches what a user would actually experience?
variants.explanation: Failure records are retained in the attempted-item denominator, because excluding them measures a different system than the one being released.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: An evaluation suite is assembled from parts with separate jobs. Item forms, scoring checks, and gate requirements each produce a different kind of evidence, and none of them substitutes for another.
variants.prompt: Match each item form to the evidence it is best suited to produce.

pairs.label: Selected response
pairs.detail: Fast breadth across many topics, scored mechanically, with distractors and option order inspected.

pairs.label: Short constructed answer
pairs.detail: Direct retrieval checked by normalized match, aliases, or numeric tolerance, keeping the raw answer.

pairs.label: Explanation or scenario
pairs.detail: Transfer judged against an observable rubric by blinded reviewers with measured agreement.

pairs.label: Grounded answer
pairs.detail: Current evidence use, scoring correctness, citation entailment, source authority, and date compliance separately.

variants.hint: Ask which failure mode each form is able to expose.
variants.explanation: The least subjective form that still represents the task is preferred, because each form exposes a different failure and none covers the others.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: An evaluation suite is assembled from parts with separate jobs. Item forms, scoring checks, and gate requirements each produce a different kind of evidence, and none of them substitutes for another.
variants.prompt: Match each scoring control to what it protects in the result.

pairs.label: Deterministic checks
pairs.detail: Decide correctness mechanically with answer keys, executable checks, schemas, units, or citation verification.

pairs.label: Calibrated judgment
pairs.detail: Validate rubrics and automated graders against blinded human review and report disagreement by slice.

pairs.label: Sampling bounds
pairs.detail: Report item counts and intervals so close scores are not ranked by point estimate alone.

pairs.label: Retained failures
pairs.detail: Keep refusals, parse errors, missing citations, tool failures, latency, and cost in the denominator.

variants.hint: Each control answers a different question about whether the number can be trusted.
variants.explanation: Mechanical correctness, grader calibration, sampling uncertainty, and failure retention are separate controls, so passing one says nothing about the others.

variants.title: Map each part to its job
variants.context: An evaluation suite is assembled from parts with separate jobs. Item forms, scoring checks, and gate requirements each produce a different kind of evidence, and none of them substitutes for another.
variants.prompt: Match each release gate requirement to the threat it addresses.

pairs.label: Critical slice lower bound
pairs.detail: Stops a thin, high-consequence slice from riding on a large general-knowledge sample.

pairs.label: Prompt variant limit
pairs.detail: Stops a result that only holds for one favorable wording of the same item.

pairs.label: Provenance and duplicate check
pairs.detail: Stops familiar or leaked items from being read as general capability.

pairs.label: Reviewer agreement floor
pairs.detail: Stops a rubric that graders interpret differently from deciding the release.

variants.hint: Name the specific way each check could otherwise be fooled.
variants.explanation: A gate is a set of predeclared checks against named threats, and missing evidence for any of them is recorded as unknown rather than counted as a pass.
